card_quote: Default disposition (sceptic seed): has seen many 'everything you know is wrong' books come and go; thinks most are reworded internet lists; default answer: no, and would not order it for the library without strong reviews. / Myth exposure: high across science, history and quotes (fact-checks misattributed quotes at work).
how_read: Cover to cover, front matter and index included, about twenty pages a night over a week. That's how I read anything I might have to recommend or order. I read the copyright page, the contents and the back matter as carefully as the stories.

w1_best.why: Six downloads before the suit, two of them by her lawyers. Precise, sourced, and genuinely surprising.
Tracing the Monte Carlo run to a 1959 book, with the newspaper archives that were searched. That's real checking.
The pyramid traced to McDermid in 1960. I'll use that one at the reference desk.
The rat bounty, set against the cobra legend. Good pairing, good source.
The bike shed committee being Parkinson's invention. My reading group would enjoy it.

w1_flat.why: Old news to anyone who uses Quote Investigator.
Same. The Twain hammer is the misattribution everyone in my line of work already knows.
Contradicts its own verdict; it shouldn't have been printed.
The Hanlon story a second time.

w1_review.headline: Sources on every page, then two pages nobody checked
w1_review.body: This is better than most 'everything you know is wrong' books: nearly every entry names its sources, and some of them, like the Streisand downloads and the Monte Carlo run, show genuine digging. But it's built on its own website's records, leans on Wikipedia more than it should, repeats several stories in pairs, and ships with no ISBN, contents entries missing page numbers, off-by-a-few page references and two stray pages, one of which contradicts its own verdict. Bottom line: not one I'd order for the library in this state, though a corrected edition might be.

w2_review_first: I'd tell a friend it's a myth quiz that does cite its sources, which puts it ahead of the usual reworded internet list. But the copy I saw wasn't ready, with stray pages, placeholders and page numbers that don't line up, and if they already know their Quote Investigator, half of it will feel familiar.

w2_lost.why: Round 2 on misattributed quotes. It's my day job; I read it out of duty.
The Franklin page. I stopped, reread it twice and put the book down for the evening.
Round 8, a run of office and software laws. Competent but dry.
The goldfish page. Second stray, and that's when I decided I couldn't recommend it as is.

w2_read_aloud.why: Everyone in my reading group has seen the pyramid in a training session. They'd enjoy learning Maslow never drew it.
The reactor in two and a half minutes and the bike shed for forty-five. Reads aloud beautifully.
One missing word, 'unmanaged'. That would start a good discussion.
A famous story with a traceable starting point, which is the whole lesson of the book.

w2_cut.why: Overlaps the Hardin entry right before it; one Hardin story is plenty.

w2_book2: If it arrives without an ISBN, without reviews and with another stray page like the goldfish, it doesn't get past my desk.
